newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Franco sees "monotonous" growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Franco sees "monotonous" growth in 1997.

text.p: Brazil's economy in 1997 will prove "even more monotonous than in 1996" but growth, foreign investment and the trade deficit would all increase, the Central Bank's International Affairs director Gustavo Franco said.
"I said 1996 would be a monotonous year and it was. 1997 will be even more monotonous," Franco told reporters.
The Central Bank's policy of gradually reducing interest rates and allowing the real currency to depreciate would continue and inflation would be under ten percent, he said.
"But 1997 will see more growth than 1996," he said.
"Average growth (throughout the year) will be significantly higher than three percent," Franco said. Three percent growth is expected for 1996.
Higher growth would lead to a bigger trade deficit than this year's expected $4.5 billion, but Franco said he saw no problem with that.
"Whether it's three, five or six (billion dollars), I don't think it's very important," he said.
Foreign direct investment, which has soared to $8.2 billion so far in 1996, would be "much higher" in 1997, thanks to upcoming privatizations, Franco said.
That should ease concerns over Brazil's current account deficit, currently just under 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, Franco said.
"All this concern about Brazil's external situation will be left further and further behind," he said.
